# Purpose

These sessions start from **what reproducible research means**, note where definitions diverge (including qualitative work), then teach everyday **workflows** that support those aims: a durable project folder, documentation, versioning, sharing boundaries, and responsible AI use.

Students organise a project folder and write documentation for **their own PhD project**, then transfer that text into the course assignment's Swedish Research Council DMP template. There is no hand-in to the team that runs these two days.

**Working definition (The Turing Way):** reproducible research is work that can be independently recreated from the **same data and the same analysis** the original team used ([definitions](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/overview/overview-definitions/)). Caveats: other fields swap the words *reproducible* and *replicable*; for much qualitative research the practical aim is often *auditability* (others can follow and evaluate how interpretations were reached), not identical findings ([Keele KORSA](https://www.keele.ac.uk/korsa/qualitative/reproducibilityreplication/)). KI does not give a formal definition; it requires documentation and openness so research can be followed, interpreted, and reproduced (see Day 1 readings).

Success criterion — the **5-year test**: someone returning in five years, the student or a colleague, can understand what was done and which decisions were made. It holds for qualitative, survey, trial, and secondary-data projects alike. Note that KI requires documentation to be stored for at least 10 years, or as long as the data is available, see the KI guidelines on data management.

Teaching time is **two afternoons of Team-Based Learning (3 h each)**, each preceded by a guided self-study morning (3 h). Day 1 afternoon is hybrid (room Future + Zoom), Day 2 is Zoom-only, so every team activity must work in breakout rooms.

# Learning outcomes

By the end of the two days, the student can:

1.  **Explain** one established definition of reproducible research (Turing Way), note where definitions diverge (including qualitative auditability), and relate that to what KI asks in its research and documentation guidelines.
2.  **Structure** a durable project folder and its documentation (README, decision log, naming and versioning) so the project passes the 5-year test.
3.  **Track** changes and decisions in a form that humans and tools can both read, and justify which versioning approach fits their project.
4.  **Draft** Swedish Research Council DMP answers on **documentation**, **data description**, **data quality**, **storage**, **security**, and **who is responsible**.
5.  **Judge** what can be shared, what must stay protected, and how to use KI-supported AI tools (Copilot-first) responsibly — with disclosure and verification.

# What happens on each day

## Day 1 — Definition, then structure and documentation

*Morning: what “reproducible” means (and where it frays), plus AI rules. Afternoon: critique synthetic folders, then build your own folder + DMP draft.*

**Morning (self-study, 3 h)**

-   Orientation: Turing Way definition + caveats (above); 5-year test; DMP assignment.
-   **AI for these sessions (before any drafting with tools):** prefer **Microsoft Copilot** (KI-supported); other tools only if they meet the same data-safety bar. Never put personal, patient, or sensitive research data in prompts. Keep prompt + output when you use AI; verify and edit before you trust it; disclose use to your team. Short pointer to [KI Generative AI and Education](https://staff.ki.se/tools-and-support/ai-at-ki/generative-ai-and-education) (full student rules and disclosure template = issue #15).
-   Read [Riktlinjer för forskning vid KI](https://medarbetare.ki.se/media/99275/download) §§6–7 (Johanna): document so research can be *spåras, tolkas och reproduceras*; openness and FAIR increase the chance to reproduce.
-   Read the [KI guidelines for research documentation and data management](https://staff.ki.se/research-support/research-data-management/plan-your-research-data-management/guidelines-for-research-documentation-and-data-management) (Johanna): reasons to document — traceability and ability to repeat analyses (reproducibility); reusability.
-   Read [Good Enough Practices](https://carpentries-lab.github.io/good-enough-practices/aio.html) (Martin): **Introduction**; **Data Management** recommendations 1–6; **Project Organization**; **Collaboration** recommendation 1 (the README).
-   FAIR: [How to FAIR](https://www.howtofair.dk/) (videos) and [KI FAIR-principles](https://staff.ki.se/research-support/research-data-management/plan-your-research-data-management/the-fair-principles) (Johanna).
-   Skim the SRC DMP template headings and the Session → SRC DMP map (six areas); individual readiness notes for iRAT.

**Afternoon (TBL, 3 h)**

-   iRAT/tRAT on concepts (Martin): definition vs KI documentation aims; raw vs derived; FAIR vs open; ELN vs project folder.
-   Application 1: Compare a good and a poor synthetic project folder (Johanna) — which workflow choices support or block reproducibility or auditability; each team posts short findings to a shared board (room + Zoom), then facilitator samples contrasts.
-   Application 2: create folder + README for *your* project (manual or Copilot under the morning AI rules); say how each choice supports the definition (or auditability). Paste **data description** and **documentation** into the DMP. Inter-team peer critique against the 5-year rubric.
-   Closing note: one improvement you will make before Day 2, and why.

## Day 2 — Versioning, sharing, and the DMP

*Workflow focus: readable history, sharing boundaries, disclosed AI use, credible DMP drafts.*

**Morning (self-study, 3 h)**

-   Read Good Enough Practices (Martin): **Keeping Track of Changes** (all); **Data Management** recommendation 7; **Collaboration** recommendations 2–5. Prefer GEP’s **Single Master Online** via **Office Online** on KI Teams/SharePoint (Google Docs fine for shared text if preferred), with regular project-folder backups (D034 / D035).
-   KI on sharing: [Share data and collaborate](https://staff.ki.se/research-support/research-data-management/collaborate-process-analyse-research-data/share-data-and-collaborate); [Policy for open access to research data](https://staff.ki.se/research-support/research-data-management/policy-for-open-access-to-research-data); **§6.1** file-naming parts and recovering earlier versions.
-   Metadata versus raw data (documentation guidelines + Day 2 GEP sections above).

**Afternoon (TBL, 3 h)**

-   iRAT/tRAT on versioning, collaboration, "as open as possible, as closed as necessary", AI disclosure.
-   Application 1: for *your* project — choose readable history (prefer Office Online + §6.1-named downloads, or dated copies + log) and state sharing/access limits; teams post short findings to a shared board. Paste **storage** and **security** into the DMP.
-   Application 2: refine folder + README / decision log (manual or Copilot); paste **data quality** and **who is responsible**. Inter-team peer critique against the 5-year rubric.
-   Closing synthesis: return to the definition and caveats; where to get KI support.

# Scope

**In scope:** a working definition of reproducible research and its limits; the workflows that support it — folder structure, documentation, versioning, sharing boundaries, responsible AI use; and the six DMP areas in outcome 4.

**Out of scope** (point to other courses or course parts, do not teach here):

-   Programming, statistics, analysis pipelines, containers, and workflow managers.
-   Git beyond a short versioning option (K8F6106 covers this).
-   The **data collection protocol** — the assignment's second component. We only note where instruments and versions live.
-   Other SRC DMP questions (legal, ethics, accessibility, long-term storage, software, DOI, costs). Students finish those for the course assignment.
-   A separate lecture on metascience or the replication crisis. Definitions and caveats stay short; depth is in the workflows.
-   A shared case vignette for applications (students work on their own PhD projects); minute-level facilitator scripts; polished video; or new TBL hosting.
